subject: PSHE & RSE
source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes and KS3 mental health lessons (Drive PSHE folder); TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27, Careers Education and Guidance Policy and RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y5 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly.

lessons.title: Managing stress and exam pressure
objectives: Explain the stress response and the difference between helpful and harmful stress
Plan revision using evidence-based techniques and a healthy routine
Apply practical and Islamic coping strategies and know when to seek help

keywords.def: the body's reaction to pressure or demand
testing yourself from memory to strengthen learning
revisiting material over time rather than cramming
an unrealistic need for everything to be perfect
trusting Allah after doing your best

starter: Bismillah. Name two signs of stress.

teach.heading: What is stress?
bullets: Adrenaline speeds up heart and breathing
A little stress can help performance
Too much for too long harms health
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain the fight-or-flight response with a simple diagram. Compare helpful stress (focus before a presentation) with overwhelming stress. Ask: ‘What are your main sources of pressure at this stage of GCSE?’ Allow pupils to answer anonymously. Link to RECIPE Resilience. Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:286, that Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Signs and triggers
bullets: Triggers: mock exams, deadlines, comparison online
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort signs into body, feelings and behaviour. Discuss triggers specific to Year 10: option subjects, controlled assessments, mocks, comparison on social media. Teach that noticing early signs helps. Misconception: if you are not stressed you do not care. Reassure pupils that calm is also compatible with high standards.

teach.heading: Study smart
bullets: Plan: timetable with fixed prayer times and breaks
Active recall: quiz yourself, use flashcards
Spaced practice: revisit after 1 day, 1 week, 1 month
Sleep 8 to 10 hours; rest helps memory
teach.note: Worked example: topic learned Monday, review on Tuesday, next Monday, and then in a month. Show a sample weekly plan with 30-40 minute work blocks and 10-minute breaks. Contrast rereading with practice questions. Mention that teenagers need around 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Link to the hadith that the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if small (Bukhari and Muslim). Link to RECIPE Progress.

teach.heading: The coping toolkit
bullets: Qur'an 65:3: whoever relies on Allah, He is sufficient
teach.note: Practise a 2-minute breathing exercise (in for 4, hold for 4, out for 6). Cite plainly: Qur'an 94:5-6 and 65:3. Explain tawakkul as effort plus trust. Discuss that unhelpful strategies include all-night revision, caffeine overload, avoidance and endless scrolling. Link to the hadith: the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, while there is good in both (Muslim).

teach.heading: Perfectionism, comparison and getting help
bullets: Compare with your past self, not others
Aim for your best, not perfect
Ask for help if stress lasts or affects daily life
teach.note: Discuss how perfectionism can lead to procrastination and anxiety. Remind pupils that grades do not measure worth. Explain how to seek help: form tutor, pastoral team, GP, NHS 111, Childline (0800 1111), Shout (text 85258), Samaritans (116 123). Emphasise that asking for help is a strength. If any pupil appears very distressed, follow safeguarding procedures.

practice: Sort into body, feelings or behaviour: (a) trouble sleeping (b) feeling tearful (c) skipping homework (d) tight shoulders.
Plan a 7-day revision schedule for one subject using spaced practice, with times for prayer and rest.
Write two kind things you could say to yourself after a poor mock result.
independent: Create a weekly revision timetable including breaks, prayers, exercise and sleep.
Write a letter to a Year 9 pupil with five tips for managing exam pressure.
Write a paragraph explaining how tawakkul and effort work together.
lessons.homework: Use active recall on one topic for 20 minutes and note how many questions you answered correctly. Plan a review for next week.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a template timetable and visual breathing guide. EAL: pre-teach study vocabulary. Stretch: research the science of memory (the forgetting curve) and apply it to your revision.

lessons.title: Healthy relationships, marriage and the law
objectives: Describe features of a healthy, committed relationship and the Islamic view of marriage
Explain that consent is essential in marriage and that forced marriage is illegal
Recognise domestic abuse and coercive control and know where to find help

keywords.def: a legal and spiritual contract between two consenting adults
a marriage without the full and free consent of both people
a pattern of behaviour that dominates and isolates a person
abusive behaviour between family members or partners
love and mercy, as in Qur'an 30:21

starter: Name two signs of an unhealthy relationship.
Name one helpline for young people.

teach.heading: What makes a healthy committed relationship?
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach in line with the TGA RSHE Policy; parents have been informed. TGA pupils live in different countries: use UK law as the baseline and remind pupils that laws vary elsewhere. Cite plainly: Qur'an 30:21, that Allah placed love and mercy between spouses. Cite the hadith that the best of you are the best to your families (Tirmidhi). Link to RECIPE Integrity and Excellence. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Marriage in Islam
bullets: Marriage is a contract based on consent
Hadith: a woman must be consulted and give permission
Parents advise and support; they do not force
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that a previously married woman must not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin must not be married until her permission is sought (Bukhari and Muslim). Teach that Islam requires free consent. Explain that families can guide with wisdom, but forcing is not permitted. Misconception: forced marriage is a religious or cultural duty. It is not.

teach.heading: The law and forced marriage
bullets: Forced marriage is a crime in England and Wales
The minimum age to marry is 18
teach.note: State clearly: since 2014 forcing someone to marry is a criminal offence in England and Wales, and since February 2023 the minimum age for marriage is 18, including for religious-only ceremonies. Explain that taking a child abroad to be married is also an offence. Pupils at risk can contact the Forced Marriage Unit, the DSL, Childline or the police. Reassure pupils that this is a protective law. If concerned about any pupil, follow safeguarding procedures the same day.

teach.heading: Domestic abuse and coercive control
bullets: Abuse can be physical, emotional, financial or online
Never the victim's fault and never acceptable
Hadith: do not harm or return harm
teach.note: Define domestic abuse and coercive control with invented examples: a partner controls money, checks messages and cuts someone off from family. Cite the hadith ‘There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm’ (Ibn Majah; Nawawi's Forty Hadith no. 32) and Qur'an 4:19 on treating spouses with kindness. Explain that abuse is not justified by religion or culture. Do not ask pupils to share their own experiences.

teach.heading: Getting help
teach.note: Share the helplines and explain they are confidential. Explain what to say: ‘I am worried about my safety or someone else's.’ Mention that FGM is also illegal in the UK and that anyone concerned should tell the DSL or contact the police; keep this factual. Close with a reminder that the school will always listen and act. Follow safeguarding procedures immediately if a concern arises.

practice: True or false? (a) In England and Wales the minimum age for marriage is 16. (b) Both people must freely consent to a marriage in Islam. (c) Coercive control can include monitoring someone's phone.
List three features of a healthy marriage from the lesson.
Write what you could say to a friend who tells you they are afraid of being forced to marry.
independent: Write a short advice leaflet: ‘Healthy relationships and the law’ with four key facts and two helplines.
Create a case study showing coercive control and the steps taken to seek help.
Write a paragraph on how Qur'an 30:21 and the hadith on consent shape Islamic marriage.
exit: Give two features of a healthy relationship.
What does UK law say about forced marriage?
lessons.homework: Write down three qualities of a healthy relationship you would look for in the future, linked to Islamic teaching.
lessons.send: SEND: provide key facts on cards and a visual of helplines. EAL: pre-teach legal vocabulary. Stretch: compare how UK law and Islamic principles each protect individuals in marriage.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Staying safe and preparing for work
lessons.title: Gambling, substances and exploitation: staying safe
objectives: Assess risk and explain why gambling, drugs and exploitation harm people
Explain how criminal exploitation (county lines) works and recognise warning signs
Know how to get help and report concerns

keywords.def: risking money on an uncertain outcome
a compulsion to continue despite harm
using someone unfairly for another's benefit
gangs using young people to move drugs between areas
gambling, forbidden in Islam

starter: Bismillah. Name two risks of vaping.
Why might someone be scared to tell an adult about a problem?

teach.heading: Thinking about risk
bullets: Risk is the chance of harm
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach a decision-making model: stop, list options, think about consequences for you and others, ask a trusted adult, decide. Ask: ‘Why do people take risks they know are harmful?’ Link to RECIPE Integrity and Resilience. Ground rules matter especially here. Use invented case studies only. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Gambling and gambling-like games
bullets: Illegal for under 18s in the UK
Can lead to debt, stress and addiction
teach.note: Worked example: a game offers a loot box for £2 with a 1% chance of a rare item. On average, a player would spend about £200 to get one. Link to Qur'an 5:90, which describes intoxicants and gambling (maysir) as abominations of Satan's handiwork. Explain that gambling harms families and finances. Misconception: you can ‘win it back’.

teach.heading: Substances: legal facts and consequences
bullets: Class A, B and C drugs: penalties can be severe
A criminal record affects work and travel
Alcohol and vapes are illegal for under 18s to buy
teach.note: Briefly revisit Y8 learning: nicotine and alcohol risks. Add legal consequences: possession and supply offences, and the way a criminal record can affect careers. Keep factual. Mention that 'legal highs' and some pills may be dangerous. Cite the hadith that Allah has prohibited whatever intoxicates (Muslim), as in Y8. Do not give detail about obtaining or using substances.

teach.heading: Criminal exploitation and county lines
bullets: Gangs groom young people with gifts or attention
Warning signs: new items, secrecy, missing school
teach.note: Explain how exploitation can start: friendly attention, gifts, favours, then pressure and debt. Show invented warning signs of a pupil being groomed. Explain that young people used by gangs are victims. Cite Qur'an 5:2, which tells believers to cooperate in righteousness and piety, not in sin and aggression. Stress that exploiters may threaten but help is available. Refer to the DSL and Prevent policy where relevant.

teach.heading: Getting help and reporting
bullets: Tell the DSL, a parent or a trusted adult
teach.note: Share routes for reporting and support. Emphasise anonymity of Crimestoppers and Fearless. GamCare’s National Gambling Helpline offers free support. Remind pupils that they will be believed and supported. Explain that anyone in immediate danger should call 999. Close by revisiting RECIPE Integrity: choosing the path of safety and truth.

practice: A game charges £1.50 per loot box. How much would 20 boxes cost? Why does the game company profit?
Spot the warning signs: ‘Sami has new trainers, a second phone and has been skipping lessons. He says a friend gives him jobs to do.’
Name two organisations that offer confidential support.
independent: Write a short guide: ‘How to spot and avoid gambling traps in games’.
Create a flowchart showing what to do if you are being pressured to carry or sell something.
Write a paragraph linking Qur'an 5:90 with protecting wealth and family.
exit: Name one warning sign of criminal exploitation.
lessons.homework: Research one support service from the lesson and write a short note describing how it helps and how to contact it.
lessons.send: SEND: use scenario cards and visual flowcharts. EAL: pre-teach legal and risk vocabulary. Stretch: analyse how game design uses reward mechanisms and propose three ethical design changes.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Staying safe and preparing for work
lessons.title: World of work: CVs, work experience and employability
objectives: Write a clear CV and plan for work experience
Explain basic rights and responsibilities at work, including health and safety, with Islamic values of amanah and ihsan

keywords.def: skills that make you suitable for work, such as teamwork
a short document summarising your education, skills and experience
a short placement in a workplace
the lowest hourly pay an employer can legally offer
trustworthiness and responsibility

starter: Bismillah. Name two skills you have.
Name one job you would like to try.

teach.heading: Employability skills
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask what employers want. Link each skill to evidence from school life: organising a charity event, leading a group project, keeping to deadlines. Cite plainly: the hadith in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things (Muslim). Link to RECIPE Integrity and Excellence. Refer to the TGA Careers Education and Guidance Policy. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Writing a CV
bullets: Contact details, profile, education, skills, experience
One page, clear headings, no spelling errors
Use evidence: ‘Led a team of 4 to raise £150’
teach.note: Show a model CV for an invented pupil, Aisha Rahman: profile sentence, GCSEs being studied, skills (Arabic, public speaking), responsibility (house captain), volunteering (food bank). Ask pupils to identify strengths. Misconception: you need paid experience; volunteering and school roles count. Remind pupils not to include sensitive personal information such as date of birth or home address online.

teach.heading: Work experience and interviews
bullets: Answer with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result
teach.note: Model a STAR answer: Situation: our class project was behind schedule. Task: I needed to organise the team. Action: I made a shared plan and checked progress. Result: we finished on time. Practise with a partner in breakout rooms. Discuss options for remote or local placements and prayer arrangements, which can be discussed politely with an employer. Mention that the careers lead can help to find placements.

teach.heading: Rights, pay and safety
bullets: Minimum wage depends on age (check gov.uk)
Under-18s have limits on hours and rest breaks
Employers must provide a safe workplace
teach.note: Explain that in April 2025 the minimum wage for under-18s was £7.55 an hour; teachers should check gov.uk for the current rate. Worked example: 6 hours at £7.55 = £45.30. Explain that employers must follow health and safety law and young workers must be supervised. Discuss reporting channels: supervisor, parent, school, ACAS or the Health and Safety Executive. Link to Qur'an 83:1-3 on fairness in dealings.

teach.heading: Work with halal values
bullets: Earn halal income by honest means
Hadith: best food is from the work of your hands (Bukhari)
teach.note: Cite plainly: the hadith that no one has eaten better food than that which he eats from the work of his own hands (Bukhari). Discuss how to remain true to values in a workplace: honesty, respect, polite negotiation for prayer breaks. Mention that the hadith of the truthful and trustworthy merchant is related by Tirmidhi. Close with a du'a for beneficial knowledge and halal provision.

practice: Turn this into a strong CV line: ‘I help in my mosque.’
Calculate pay: 5 hours at £7.55 an hour.
Write a STAR answer to: ‘Tell me about a time you worked in a team.’
independent: Write your first CV using the template: profile, education, skills, responsibilities and interests.
Write a letter asking a local business for work experience.
Write a paragraph on how amanah and ihsan help you at work.
lessons.homework: Complete your CV and ask a parent or carer to give one piece of feedback. Write what you changed.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a CV template and sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach CV vocabulary. Stretch: research one employer, prepare three interview questions and a STAR answer.
